script.base: Spread and total were not saved, so the script is inferred only from weeks 1-2 form. Carolina's pass game is the engine: Coker and McMillan each have 18 targets, and Bryce Young is better off the blitz (0.37 EPA/dropback, n not blitzed vs 0.18 vs blitz, n=24) against a Cleveland blitz rate of only 19%. Cleveland's dropback game is the fragile side: Watson is -0.20 EPA vs blitz (n=29) and Carolina blitzes 44%, so CLE is likelier to lean on Watson's legs (11 carries, 62 yards) and short targets than on Boston shot volume. Neither back is a proven clock-killer yet (Hubbard 22 carries/102 yards; Judkins 24/54) even though both run defenses leak (CLE 4.93 YPC, CAR 6.31).
script.flip1: Carolina gets ahead and Hubbard's carries jump well above his 11-per-game pace against CLE's 4.93 YPC and 9 runs of 10+, so Coker and McMillan fall to 4 or fewer targets and both receiving overs die.
script.flip2: Carolina's 44% blitz does not wreck Watson (his no-blitz EPA is already 0.27), Boston's 174 air yards cash, and the game becomes a shootout or a CLE-leaning script where Carolina never sustains the 9-target WR roles from weeks 1-2.

matchup.overlap: CAR's co-primary targets, Coker (18 tgt, 204 rec yds, 172 air) and McMillan (18 tgt, 176 rec yds, 251 air), overlap a CLE defense that rarely blitzes and has already allowed 7 passes of 20+. That is the core edge. CLE's top option Boston (11 tgt, 154 yds, 174 air) overlaps the wrong trait: CAR's 44% blitz, where Watson's EPA is negative. Judkins' 24 carries overlap CAR's 6.31 YPC, but his own 2.25 YPC has not cashed it.

pre_mortem: It's Monday and both overs lost because the two-game spike did not travel: Coker's 204 yards on 172 air yards was one or two YAC plays, McMillan's 251 air yards again failed to convert (only 176 receiving yards so far), and Carolina either led and handed Hubbard more than 11 carries against a CLE run defense allowing 4.93 YPC and 9 runs of 10+, or Cleveland's 19% blitz ticked up and Young was forced off his 0.37 no-blitz EPA. A late scratch not in this pack, or CLE simply bracketing the two 18-target receivers, also loses both legs together. That clock-kill flip is real, but it is one path, not the base read, and the yardage gaps (102 vs 59, 88 vs 62.5) are why the legs stay.
slip_story: One story only: Carolina pass volume vs a low-blitz Cleveland defense. Coker over 59 and McMillan over 62.5 win together if Young stays in his no-blitz environment and both keep a 6-plus target share. Do not mix this slip with a game-total under, a Hubbard rush over, or a Carolina clock-kill stack. CLE pass overs (Boston) need the opposite pressure story and stay off this ticket.
